intro: In this college you'll learn the Dutch of official life: separating your rubbish, going to the town hall, arranging things online with DigiD, and understanding basic insurance, all in the polite 'u' register.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome to official life
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme sixteen. Its title is [[Goed geregeld]], which means 'well arranged', and when something is sorted out properly a Dutch person will say with satisfaction [[Dat is goed geregeld.]] In the Netherlands a lot of daily life is admin: the rubbish, the town hall, your insurance, official letters. The good news is that there is a small, repeating set of words and you only have to learn it once. The most important grammar today is the polite word [[u]], which you use with officials, with strangers, and with anyone you want to respect. With [[u]] the verb looks just like the 'he/she' form, so you say [[u kunt]], you say [[u heeft]], and you say [[u woont]]. The second big idea is the verb [[moeten]], which means 'must' or 'have to', because so much Dutch admin you simply have to do yourself. You will hear sentences like [[Dat moet u zelf regelen.]] In this college I explain everything in clear English, but every Dutch phrase is spoken by a native voice, so please repeat each one out loud. Ready? [[Laten we beginnen!]]

paragraphs.heading: Separating your waste
paragraphs.text: Let's start with something you do every single day: the rubbish, which is [[het afval]]. The Dutch are famous for separating it, and the verb for that is [[afval scheiden]]. A neighbour might proudly explain [[In Nederland scheiden we het afval.]] There are a few main streams to learn. Vegetable, fruit and garden waste is [[gft]], the green stream. Paper and cardboard is [[papier]]. Plastic packaging is [[plastic]]. Glass bottles and jars are [[glas]]. And everything that is left over is [[restafval]], the residual waste. Each stream has its own bin or container, which is [[de container]]. A very practical question to know is [[Waar gooi je het in?]], meaning 'where do you throw it in?'. Or more politely [[Waar moet ik dit weggooien?]], 'where do I have to throw this away?'. The answer often uses a colour, for example [[Het glas gaat in de groene container.]] Glass also goes to a bottle bank, the [[glasbak]], which you find in many streets. One warm tip: ask a neighbour which day the bins go out, because there is usually a fixed collection day, and getting it right is a small but real way to show you belong here.

paragraphs.heading: The town hall and appointments
paragraphs.text: Now to the heart of Dutch officialdom: the town hall, which is [[het gemeentehuis]], run by your local council, the [[gemeente]]. You go there for big life things like a passport, [[het paspoort]], or to register a move. The golden rule is that you almost always need an appointment first, [[de afspraak]]. So a key sentence is [[Ik wil een afspraak maken bij de gemeente.]], 'I want to make an appointment at the council'. At the desk the clerk, the [[ambtenaar]], will usually first ask [[Heeft u een afspraak gemaakt?]], 'have you made an appointment?'. This is where your polite requests shine. To ask for help you say [[Kunt u mij helpen, alstublieft?]], with that formal 'please', [[alstublieft]]. If you do not understand, the softer, very polite form is [[Zou u dat kunnen uitleggen?]], 'could you explain that?'. And a useful one when collecting something is [[Ik kom mijn paspoort ophalen.]], 'I am coming to collect my passport'. There is even a comforting Dutch saying for this: [[Een afspraak maken kost niets.]], 'making an appointment costs nothing', so never be shy about booking one.

paragraphs.heading: You have to arrange it online
paragraphs.text: Here is a sentence you will meet constantly: [[Dat moet u online regelen.]], which means 'you have to arrange that online'. Modern Dutch admin lives on the internet, and the key to it all is your [[DigiD]], pronounced 'dee-gee-dee'. This is your personal digital login for government websites, and you really must apply for one early. Notice the pattern with [[moeten]]: the council puts the main verb right at the end as an infinitive. So you hear [[U moet uw verhuizing online doorgeven.]], 'you have to report your move online', where [[doorgeven]] means 'to report' or 'pass on'. Or [[U kunt uw paspoort online aanvragen.]], 'you can apply for your passport online', with [[aanvragen]] for 'apply for'. Three verbs unlock most tasks: [[regelen]] is 'to arrange', [[aanvragen]] is 'to apply for', and [[doorgeven]] is 'to report'. On a website you log in like this: [[Log in met uw DigiD.]] Then you fill in your details, your [[gegevens]], and afterwards you usually receive a confirmation, [[de bevestiging]], by email. A handy question to check is [[Moet ik dit online regelen?]], 'do I have to arrange this online?'. If not, the relieved answer you hope for is [[Dat hoeft niet.]], 'that is not necessary'.

paragraphs.heading: Insurance you must arrange yourself
paragraphs.text: Let's talk about insurance, which is [[de verzekering]], because in the Netherlands much of it you arrange yourself. The most important by far is health insurance, [[de zorgverzekering]], and it is legally required for almost everyone living here. So you will often hear the firm sentence [[De verzekering moet u zelf regelen.]], 'you have to arrange the insurance yourself'. A natural question to ask an advisor or a friend is [[Ben ik goed verzekerd?]], 'am I well insured?'. To apply, you can ask [[Hoe vraag ik een verzekering aan?]], 'how do I apply for insurance?', again using that verb [[aanvragen]]. When you sign up, you often need to sign, and your signature is your [[handtekening]]. Forms will ask for personal [[gegevens]] and sometimes a confirmation, [[de bevestiging]], will follow. A practical phrase for any office is [[Welke documenten moet ik meenemen?]], 'which documents do I have to bring?', where [[meenemen]] means 'to bring along'. Compare it with insurance for your home or liability, but the health one comes first. Remember the reassuring Dutch saying [[Komt voor elkaar.]], 'it will be taken care of'. Arranging insurance feels heavy at first, but once it is done you can truly say [[Dat is goed geregeld.]]

paragraphs.heading: At the desk — you can do this
paragraphs.text: Let's put it together at the council desk. Imagine you have moved and want to register. You begin politely: [[Goedemiddag. Ik ben verhuisd en wil mijn nieuwe adres doorgeven.]], 'good afternoon, I have moved and want to report my new address'. The clerk asks [[Heeft u een afspraak gemaakt?]] You did not know, so you say honestly [[Sorry, dat wist ik niet. Moet ik dat online doen?]], 'sorry, I did not know that, do I have to do that online?'. The clerk nods and explains [[Ga naar de website van de gemeente en log in met uw DigiD.]], 'go to the council's website and log in with your DigiD'. You ask which details to enter: [[Welke gegevens moet ik invullen?]] The answer: [[Vul uw oude en nieuwe adres in.]], 'fill in your old and new address'. Finally you check [[Moet ik daarna nog langskomen?]], and you are relieved to hear [[Nee, dat hoeft niet. U krijgt een bevestiging per e-mail.]] See how far you have come! With [[u]], with [[moeten]], and with a few key verbs, you can handle the rubbish, the town hall, the websites, and your insurance. [[Heel goed gedaan!]] Well done — I will see you in theme seventeen!
